item.title: China's state television airs rare footage of PLA anti-drone laser, microwave equipment in live-fire drills
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04 20:01:00
Counter-drone units of China’s People’s Liberation Army operate in combat-oriented training Photo: Screenshot of CCTV News China's state television CCTV News on Sunday released rare footage of the People's Liberation Army (PLA) Army's counter-drone units in combat-oriented training, highlighting laser weapons, integrated missile-gun systems and high-power microwave weapons as an "iron triangle" of anti-drone equipment. China's drone capabilities and counter-drone technologies are among the world's most advanced after years of development, Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Sunday. He said the footage also showed how realistic training was helping refine the use of these weapons. According to CCTV News, a brigade of the PLA's 75th Group Army conducted live-fire tactical drills involving multiple scenarios from daytime into the night, testing rapid response, firepower and sustained combat capabilities. During the drills, CCTV News reported that air-defense units were assembled and deployed to designated positions after receiving orders to move. Radar then detected a dense swarm of drones approaching at extremely low altitude. Counter-drone units activated ground-based laser and microwave systems, using optical dazzling and electromagnetic suppression to disrupt the swarm's formation. Interceptor drones took off to engage targets that broke through, followed by anti-aircraft gunfire against the remaining drones, CCTV reported. Jia Jingcheng, a PLA Army serviceman quoted by CCTV, said the exercise focused on coordinating different types of air-defense equipment. It tested personnel's ability to assess complex aerial threats, respond to unexpected situations and combine multiple methods of attack to address weaknesses in combat readiness. Immediately after the first engagement, exercise controllers declared that the troops' defensive position had been exposed, they were forced to withdraw their equipment, relocate and rapidly establish a new position, redeploying weapons and camouflage to restore their air defenses. Radar units were networked to provide early warning and real-time tracking. As the exercise continued late into the night, units switched to nighttime operations, with radar, electro-optical and infrared equipment continuing to search for aerial targets, the report said. He Qing, another PLA Army serviceman quoted by CCTV, said the drills combined responses to different aerial threats with battlefield maneuvering and the handling of unexpected situations in an unfamiliar, complex Gobi Desert environment. The aim was to strengthen rapid reaction, mobile defense and sustained readiness under both daytime and nighttime conditions. Alongside the exercise footage, CCTV explained the complementary roles of the three types of counter-drone equipment. Laser weapons use high-energy beams to damage airborne drones, while integrated missile-gun systems provide terminal defense against small, slow and low-flying targets. The missile-gun system shown in the footage features a centrally mounted six-barrel rotary cannon and four short-range air-defense missile launchers alongside it. It combines dense gunfire with precision missile strikes and can operate independently or as part of a networked air-defense system, according to CCTV. The high-power microwave system shown uses an eight-wheel-drive chassis, with a large panel and a detection radar mounted at the rear. CCTV said the weapon releases microwave pulses that damage a drone's internal electronic components, causing it to fail and fall. While lasers engage individual targets, microwave weapons can affect a wider area and engage multiple drones in a swarm, helping counter attacks designed to overwhelm defenses, the broadcaster said. Supported by radar, electro-optical sensors and electronic detection equipment, these weapons form part of a layered defense system combining long-range early warning, electronic suppression and close-range interception, CCTV reported. The development of such systems addresses challenges that inexpensive drones pose to conventional air defenses. Drones have relatively low barriers to development and procurement, allowing even countries and armed groups with limited technological capabilities to obtain them, Chinese military affairs expert Zhang Xuefeng was quoted by CCTV as saying. Their low cost permits large-scale use, while their small size, low flight altitude and limited radar signatures make detection and interception difficult, Zhang said. Conventional defenses can consequently struggle to detect drones, intercept them affordably and stop them effectively. Long-range air-defense missiles can cost millions of dollars each, while short-range missiles can cost tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars, Zhang noted. Using them against inexpensive drones creates an unfavorable cost exchange, compounded by limits on missile production. China has responded by developing a broad range of counter-drone systems and interception weapons, Song told the Global Times. He said the diversity and sophistication of its equipment reflected years of attention to both drone development and the threats drones create. China had placed considerable emphasis on drones before the Russia-Ukraine conflict, and the conflict further deepened its understanding of their battlefield role, Song said. Alongside advances in drone applications, China has also prioritized the development and use of counter-drone equipment. China's counter-drone equipment have developed alongside its drones, incorporating increasingly advanced technologies, Song said. He added that China would continue testing the equipment under realistic combat conditions to optimize its use.

item.title: DPP dangerously expels Chinese mainland fishing vessels; provocations must bring due consequences: Hai Feng
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04 19:57:00
Illustration: Xia Qing/GT October 1 marked the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China. On this solemn day, Taiwan region's "Coast Guard Administration (CGA)" used high-pressure water cannons against a fishing boat from the Chinese mainland in waters near the Dongsha Islands, disabling the vessel's power system and leaving its crew stranded at sea for a time. No rhetorical whitewashing can hide this reckless disregard for human life Though the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) has framed the operation as a so-called "lawful expulsion", facts can never be altered by rhetorical embellishment. Cross-Straits fishermen have long operated in relevant waters, forming established traditional fishing grounds. Against the normal temporary fishing activities of civilian vessels, the DPP dispatched large official patrol ships and continuously fired high-pressure water cannons at close range toward the vessel's wheelhouse. The reckless operations caused the boat to lose power and left crew members stranded at sea. Such excessive handling goes far beyond reasonable law-enforcement limits, and carries clear elements of danger, coercion and provocation. Maritime conditions are complex and volatile, and vessel equipment can malfunction at any time. Continuous use of high-pressure water cannons from a large patrol ship at close range against a civilian fishing vessel poses substantial risks to the hull, power systems and crew safety. Should a serious accident occur, no explanations after the fact can reverse the outcome or remedy the harm suffered by the families of those involved. Taiwan's CGA claimed it deliberately avoided crew members on the deck while spraying water, yet such arguments in no way justify its dangerous conduct. If the Taiwan side was fully aware that high-pressure water cannons carry injury risks, why did it keep firing toward the vessel's wheelhouse? Proceeding with the operation despite knowing the risks reveals cold disregard for the life and safety of fishermen from the mainland. Ordinary residents from the mainland head out to sea for fishing or recreational activities, yet the DPP treats them as targets to project a tough stance. Using civilian vessels from the mainland as props for political posturing and wagering the safety of ordinary people as bargaining chips in confrontation is outrageous. Post-rescue actions cannot offset responsibility for risks created beforehand The DPP has deliberately highlighted the so-called "humanitarian rescue" carried out by the Yunlin after the fishing boat lost power, including boarding operations and supply provision. However, this does not exempt them from liabilities over their earlier handling. It was the impact of high-pressure water cannons that disabled the vessel's power system and left mainland crew members stranded at sea in peril. Post-incident remedies cannot alter the objective fact that the danger had already materialized, nor erase the fright and hardship endured by the mainland fishermen on the water. At its core, this incident is a tangible manifestation of the DPP's long-standing confrontational agenda. In recent years, ignoring the history and reality of cross-Straits fishermen operating in these waters for generations, the DPP has repeatedly framed normal maritime activities from the mainland as alleged security threats, wrapping ordinary fishery issues in political and security narratives. As a result, the atmosphere of maritime standoffs across the Taiwan Straits keeps escalating, and the rights and interests of fishermen on both sides of the Straits have suffered severe damage. Anger must translate into well-calibrated countermeasures. It is fully understandable that netizens from the mainland are outraged by this provocative incident perpetrated by the DPP. The mainland's capacity to safeguard national sovereignty and people's rights and interests is vastly stronger than before. Faced with maritime provocations, the mainland has ample capabilities and a range of tools to defend its legitimate rights and interests, enabling reciprocal, targeted, steady and effective countermeasures. On the basis of preserving evidence, verifying facts and clarifying accountability, China will pursue legal accountability where warranted, and keep up efforts to uphold rights as appropriate. Countermeasures target the dangerous provocative acts and the responsible parties behind them, and are meant to protect the personal safety and legitimate rights and interests of people on both sides of the Taiwan Straits. The mainland does not equate the DPP's confrontational agenda with the will of Taiwan compatriots. Still less will we force ordinary people in Taiwan to bear the costs of political confrontation. Warnings must be heard, countermeasures must be forceful, and accountability must be imposed on specific responsible parties. The Chinese mainland's resolve to protect people's legitimate rights and interests, oppose dangerous provocations and crack down on "Taiwan independence" separatist acts remains unshakable. Anyone who recklessly endangers the lives and property of ordinary people must face serious consequences. Anyone bent on undermining peace and stability across the Taiwan Straits must bear full consequences for their actions. The momentum toward reunification is irresistible. Every provocation by "Taiwan independence" separatist forces will bring our countermeasures one step forward, steadily advancing the process of national reunification.

item.title: 20th Asian Games close in Nagoya
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04 17:57:00
Fireworks explode during the closing ceremony of the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Oct. 4, 2026. (Photo: Xinhua) The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games came to a close Sunday after a two-week competition, with China topping the gold medal table for the 12th consecutive edition. China finished with 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals, its best haul at an overseas Asiad. Japan ranked second with 83 gold, 95 silver and 91 bronze medals, followed by South Korea with 39 gold, 43 silver and 68 bronze medals. Thai sprinter Puripol Boonson and Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi were named the men's and women's Most Valuable Players of the Games.

item.title: China's security ministry warns of genetic resource theft and cross-border biosecurity risks
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04 16:37:00
Photo: Screenshot from the WeChat account of China’s Ministry of State Security China's Ministry of State Security warned on Sunday that some overseas organizations have entered ecologically sensitive areas under the guise of tourism or scientific research, or illegally collected human blood samples through purported medical testing to steal China's genetic resources and research data. In a post on its official WeChat account during the National Day holiday, the ministry highlighted cases involving blood samples, exotic pets and plant seeds, calling for greater public awareness of biosecurity risks associated with moving biological materials across borders. The ministry cited a series of major smuggling cases involving pregnant women's blood samples uncovered by Guangzhou Customs in 2025. Authorities dismantled an illicit cross-border network spanning 23 provinces, helping protect China's human genetic resources, it said. The warning also addressed the growing popularity of exotic pets and repeated attempts to bring them into China without permission. Customs authorities intercepted 5,439 batches of non-native species in passenger baggage, mail and other inbound channels in 2025, according to the ministry. In the first quarter of 2026 alone, customs authorities intercepted more than 1,000 exotic pets, including beetles, spiders, frogs, salamanders, lizards and snakes. Moving such live animals and specimens across borders requires quarantine and approval procedures, the ministry said. Plants and seeds present similar concerns. Some people buy unusual flowers or seeds overseas for personal use, while others take native seedlings and seeds abroad as gifts, overlooking the requirements governing their movement, the ministry said. In May, customs officers found 50 packets of mixed seeds in a mailed parcel declared as "personal belongings." Each packet weighed 500 grams, and the shipment contained large quantities of cannabis seeds. Customs authorities have also uncovered cases in which travelers concealed plant seedlings or disguised them as gifts to bring them into China without declaring them or submitting them for quarantine, the ministry said. Such cases carry risks beyond individual violations. Illegal imports of non-native species and unauthorized exports of native organisms or genetic resources can disrupt ecosystems, threaten agricultural production and public health and undermine biosecurity, the ministry said. It described biological genetic resources as national strategic resources and warned of the implications of their illegal export. China subjects animals, plants, related products and other regulated items moving across its borders to quarantine approval, inspection and supervision, the ministry said, warning that concealment and false declarations could seriously endanger national security. The ministry called on travelers not to carry animals, plants, seeds or other biological materials across borders without authorization. Those importing or exporting biological materials for research, teaching or other purposes should obtain the necessary permits in advance from customs and relevant agricultural or science and technology authorities, declare the materials accurately and submit them for quarantine. Members of the public should report suspected illegal cross-border movements of biological materials to the relevant authorities and assist with investigations, it added. Global Times

item.title: US-set agenda items on 'overcapacity,' forced labor fail to yield consensus at G20 trade meeting: MOFCOM
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04 13:33:00
The Ministry of Commerce of China File photo: VCG The G20 Trade Ministers' Meeting produced no outcome documents on three agenda items set by the US presidency — addressing "overcapacity", eliminating "forced labor" and adjusting the most-favored-nation (MFN) treatment principle — while members reached a joint statement on opposing the weaponization of food, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) said. The spokesperson made the remarks on Sunday when asked for China's comment and about it contribution to the meeting which was held in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, the US, from September 30 to October 1. The overcapacity and forced labor agenda items had been highly contentious from the outset, the spokesperson said. G20 members are currently subject to additional Section 301 tariffs related to forced labor, and many are also targets of Section 301 investigations into overcapacity. Against this backdrop, many members expressed differing views on the presidency's inclusion of these issues on the agenda and its efforts to promote joint statements and establish cooperation mechanisms. Ultimately, as most members held differing views, the meeting was unable to reach agreement on outcome documents on the relevant issues, the spokesperson said. China noted that the chair's statement issued by the US after the meeting said that the US, together with two other G20 members, had issued a statement on forced labor outside the G20 framework, the spokesperson said. On the agenda item concerning adjustments to the MFN treatment principle, the overwhelming majority of members, including China, emphasized during discussions that the principle is the cornerstone of the multilateral trading system and provides stability and predictability for global trade. Any weakening of the principle would seriously undermine the foundations of the multilateral trading system, the spokesperson said. In line with members' views, the presidency did not put forward a proposal for an outcome document on this issue. At the meeting, members exchanged views on the agenda items set by the US presidency — opposing the weaponization of food, addressing overcapacity, eliminating forced labor and adjusting the MFN treatment principle — and reached a joint statement on the food issue, while no outcome documents were produced on the other issues, the spokesperson said. During consultations on the food issue, many emerging-market and developing members, including China, proposed that food-importing and food-exporting countries should jointly maintain the stability of food supply chains, while all parties have the right to take measures in pursuit of domestic public policy objectives and safeguard food security, the spokesperson said. The presidency took these views into consideration, which were fully reflected in the joint statement. This outcome was the result of consensus and joint efforts by all G20 members, the spokesperson said. Throughout the meeting, China maintained an open and cooperative attitude, participated constructively in discussions on all agenda items and communicated closely with other members, fully playing its role in facilitating dialogue and cooperation, the spokesperson said. At the same time, China remained firm in its principles, resolutely safeguarded its own interests and the common interests of developing countries, and worked to promote G20 unity and cooperation. Looking ahead to the upcoming G20 Miami Summit, China is willing to work with the presidency and all members, uphold the principle of consensus, strengthen unity and cooperation, and jointly contribute positive and pragmatic economic and trade outcomes to the summit, the spokesperson said. Global Times

item.title: A taste of home in orbit: How China keeps its astronauts well-fed
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04 07:21:00
This image captured at Beijing Aerospace Control Center on May 25, 2026 shows a group picture of the crew of Shenzhou-21 and Shenzhou-23 spaceships. (Xinhua/Jin Liwang) Although called Tiangong, or "Heavenly Palace," China's space station is becoming less distant and more like home, as astronauts bring the comforting tastes into orbit. The Chinese space kitchen now serves nearly 200 food items. Alongside dumplings and mooncakes, home-style dishes such as Kung Pao chicken, mapo tofu and fried rice have made it onto the station's menu. Videos showing astronauts savoring freshly cooked meat and cakes in orbit have gone viral. Their smiling faces and bright eyes make the aroma almost leap off the screen. Yang Liwei, the country's first astronaut, joked at a recent press conference that he was envious. He said astronauts can now use air-frying equipment in space and enjoy baked chicken wings in orbit. During his Shenzhou-5 mission in 2003, which lasted less than one day, his diet was limited to packaged instant food that could not be heated. Microgravity, cosmic radiation and the enclosed cabin environment impose strict requirements on space diets. Floating particles and droplets may drift into instruments and trigger malfunctions. Since Yuri Gagarin, the first human to travel into space, paste-like food and compressed energy bars had long served as the standard meals for astronauts. In June 2013, Wang Yaping, together with two fellow male crewmates, carried out the 15-day Shenzhou-10 space mission. People remembered this female astronaut with a ponytail for her space lecture. At the same time, the image of her floating a "zongzi," a leaf-wrapped rice dumpling, by hand also left a deep impression on the public. Zongzi is traditionally enjoyed during the Dragon Boat Festival, which happened to coincide with the Shenzhou-10 mission that year. To help the astronauts celebrate, this special snack was added to the spaceship pantry. Students watch Wang Yaping (R) demonstrating drinking water in China's space station, at the China Science and Technology Museum in Beijing, capital of China, Dec. 9, 2021. (Xinhua/Jin Liwang) Eight years later, Wang spent Spring Festival aboard the Tiangong space station during the Shenzhou-13 mission. It is also China's first six-month-long space stay. Scientists customized the cuisine: for instance, they prepared dumplings with seafood fillings because Wang grew up by the sea, and plenty of spicy food for crew member Ye Guangfu, who was born in chili-obsessed Sichuan Province. At that time, the core module Tianhe had several sections, including those for working, sleeping, dining and exercising. The videos of Shenzhou-13 crew practicing calligraphy and playing Taichi became social media hits. China completed the construction of its space station in 2022, with one core module and two lab modules forming a 110-square-meter orbital structure. Oxygen can be fully regenerated, and water recovery exceeds 95 percent. Since then, long-duration spaceflights have become routine, and the Chinese "space home" can host up to six astronauts in orbit at a time. Space residency is also set to last even longer. One member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, currently aboard the Tiangong, will conduct a one-year in-orbit stay. Moreover, as China pushes further into deep-space exploration, these extended stays will become the norm, which means astronauts' diets will be more important than ever. This screen image captured at Beijing Aerospace Control Center on April 16, 2026 shows Shenzhou-21 astronaut Wu Fei performing extravehicular activities outside China's orbiting space station.(Photo by Zhang Fan/Xinhua) Because weightlessness causes bone calcium loss and muscle atrophy, space food must be high in calcium and protein, low in sodium and balanced in dietary fiber. According to the Astronaut Center of China, researchers have developed space food that counteracts oxidative damage, supports immunity, reduces fatigue and regulates the gut microbiome. But taste is another problem. In microgravity, blood shifts upward, causing nasal congestion and cutting smell sensitivity by at least 30 percent. Since taste is closely tied to smell, astronauts often find food bland. The center's researchers have responded with adding more strong-flavored dishes, with liquid soy sauce and concentrated chili sauce. New technology has also played a big role in keeping astronauts well-fed. The astronaut center, in collaboration with private companies, has upgraded the "space kitchen" with a suite of intelligent appliances for drinking water, food reheating and baking. This allows astronauts in orbit to enjoy hot meals within 20 minutes, rather than waiting longer or eating cold food. Liu Weibo, an expert with the center, gave an example of the hot-air baking oven, which is a pioneering Chinese design for space use that can efficiently remove cooking fumes and allow astronauts to enjoy barbecue in orbit. During a space lecture for Hong Kong and Macao students last month, Shenzhou-23 crew member Li Jiaying, or Lai Ka-ying in Cantonese, showed freshly baked cakes and said they reminded her of egg waffles, a popular snack from her hometown. She is a Hong Kong local. Students attend a live space lecture of the "Tiangong Class" Hong Kong and Macao Designated Session in Hong Kong, south China, Sept. 9, 2026.(Photo by Lui Sui Wai/Xinhua) Space food supplies have also become more diverse and nutritious, including more fruits and vegetables, as well as frozen steak and chicken wings. The next-generation cargo craft Qingzhou, designed for future in-orbit supply delivery, will have greater cold-chain transport capacity. However, long-term space residency requires reducing dependence on Earth's supplies, said center expert Bian Qiang. "The controlled ecological life-support tests we are conducting are intended to build an ecosystem in space that regenerates water, air and food on site, to reduce extraterrestrial survival's dependence on Earth resupply and ultimately achieve self-sufficiency." Since the Shenzhou-16 mission in 2023, China has been growing plants in orbit. It has tested more than 20 varieties from 14 plant species, including lettuce, carrots, potatoes and wheat. The Shenzhou-18 crew in 2024 was tasked with raising fish in an "aquarium" to study how space affects their growth. Scientists said the work may one day allow astronauts to enjoy fish from their own in-orbit harvests. Photo taken on Feb. 26, 2021 shows sprouting rice seeds that had made a round trip to the moon aboard the Chang'e-5 probe at the central greenhouse of the National Engineering Research Center of Plant Space Breeding of the South China Agricultural University in Guangzhou of south China's Guangdong Province. (Xinhua/Liu Dawei) China is targeting a crewed lunar landing by 2030. Living on the moon will make resupply much more challenging because of the increased distance from Earth. "We plan to build a Chinese 'lunar vegetable garden' on the moon," Bian said. From heating, baking to farming, feeding astronauts well in space is not a luxury. It is part of the mission, bringing a taste of home to the universe.

item.title: China ready to work with all parties for fruitful APEC 'China Year': Chinese FM on Putin's remarks about trilateral meeting
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03 21:10:00
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun As the host for this year's APEC, China stands ready to work with all parties for a fruitful APEC "China Year" and make new contributions to the economic growth of the Asia Pacific and beyond, a spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry said on Saturday, when asked to comment on Russian President Vladimir Putin's remarks about a possible trilateral meeting with the Chinese and US leaders. Putin said that it is possible to have a trilateral meeting with Chinese and US leaders during the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting and it's beneficial to exchange views and understand each other's positions through the meeting. He also emphasized the need to understand what the parties would discuss at the meeting, according to TASS. Asked about China's comment, Guo Jiakun, the spokesperson, also said that "as for your specific question, I have no information to offer at the moment." Also asked about the Russian leader's reported remarks that he believes his meeting with the Chinese leader at the APEC summit in China next month will yield results, Guo said that the strategic guidance provided by head-of-state diplomacy serves as the most important political underpinning for the steady and sustained advancement of China-Russia relations. "China welcomes President Putin's attendance at the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen this November and stands ready to work with the Russian side for fruitful outcomes of the APEC 'China Year,'" Guo said. Global Times

item.title: Chinese PLA completes Russia's Center-2026 exercise with 99A tanks, unmanned systems; expert highlights lessons from modern warfare
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03 17:02:00
A Chinese PLA Type 99A main battle tank fires during the Center-2026 exercise. Photo: China Military Bugle’s official Sina Weibo account Chinese troops have completed their participation in Russia's Center-2026 (Tsentr-2026) exercise and begun withdrawing after joint training with forces from multiple countries wrapped up with a closing ceremony in Chelyabinsk on Friday, with the drills focusing on intelligence reconnaissance, command and control, fire strikes and comprehensive support, according to the PLA Daily. The Chinese forces were drawn from the PLA Central Theater Command and deployed to the Chebarkul training ground in Russia through a combination of motorized movement, railway transport and air transport. During the field-training phase, the troops practiced three-dimensional reconnaissance, integrated information-fire strikes, guided entry, multi-directional assaults and rapid pursuit and annihilation, the report said. Photos released by the PLA's official media account China Military Bugle showed Type 99A main battle tanks of the Chinese contingent taking part in the exercise. The Type 99A is a main battle tank currently in service with the PLA Army and has previously appeared in major Chinese military exercises. Unmanned equipment also featured prominently in the exercise. China Central Television (CCTV) News reported on Saturday that drone "swarms" provided ground combat groups with precise target information, while tactical drones, attack helicopters and unmanned ground vehicles worked together to strike simulated frontline targets. Small groups also conducted multi-wave fire assaults from multiple directions against defensive positions. According to official Telegram account of the Russian Ministry of Defense, Russian Defense Minister Andrey Belousov said earlier that preparations for Center-2026 took into account what Russia described as the "unique experience" gained from its "special military operation," as well as the features of combat operations in modern armed conflicts. A report from CCTV News citing Russian reports on the final stage of the exercise also said the exercise tasks drew on experience from the special military operation. One important value of the exercise for the PLA is the opportunity to draw lessons from the combat experience accumulated by participating countries, Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Saturday. "In addition to experiences drawn from the Russian troops, countries such as Pakistan and some Central Asian participants also have experience from years of counterterrorism operations," Song said. "By training together, the participating militaries can learn from each other's strengths and improve their respective capabilities," the expert added. Song noted that recent conflicts have also highlighted growing threats to traditional armored formations. Instead of the large-scale armored clashes seen in earlier wars, tanks and other armored vehicles are now vulnerable to attacks from large numbers of drones as well as precision-guided weapons. For the PLA, studying the difficulties and losses encountered by armored forces in recent conflicts can help improve its ability to respond to such asymmetric threats, the expert said. The combination of Type 99A main battle tanks with drones and unmanned ground vehicles during the exercise also reflects the growing integration of traditional manned platforms with unmanned systems, Song pointed out. Unmanned systems can conduct reconnaissance or undertake higher-risk missions ahead of manned forces, helping reduce risks to personnel and crewed equipment, while also extending the reconnaissance and targeting reach of armored formations, Song said. Such coordination could allow platforms including the Type 99A to operate more effectively while improving their battlefield survivability. The PLA Daily said the high-intensity exercise, conducted in unfamiliar terrain overseas and in a multinational environment, tested the Chinese troops' capabilities in long-range strategic deployment, cross-border logistics support and joint operational command. Chinese forces participated at multiple levels, ranging from exercise scenario design and operational command to field training. Following the exercise, the Chinese troops began withdrawing from the Chebarkul training ground by air and railway. The PLA Daily said the troops will review their experience in multinational operational planning, joint live-force operations, long-distance cross-border deployment and operational coordination after returning to their units.

item.title: Why are two fighter jets – delivered three-years late – causing such excitement within the DPP? : Hai Feng
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03 13:29:00
US Taiwan arms sales Illustration: Liu Rui/GT On October 2, two F-16V fighter jets – originally scheduled for delivery three years ago – arrived at the Chihhang Air Base in Taitung, Taiwan region. The arrival of the new fighter jets in Taiwan acted like a shot of adrenaline for the DPP, sending the party into a state of high excitement. However, clear-eyed observers on the island have pointed out the stark reality: Despite paying a staggering sum of over NT$240 billion ($7.54 billion) for 66 fighter jets, and after numerous twists and turns, a mere two aircraft have actually arrived. Why has such a delayed, exorbitantly expensive, and limited initial delivery been packaged by the DPP authorities as a "major achievement" worthy of grand celebration? The answer may well be that, for the DPP, these two fighter jets have long since ceased to be about so-called "defense" and have become, entirely, a long-awaited political performance. Arrival of two fighter jets in Taiwan cannot mask three-year delay According to reports by Taiwan media, Taiwan procured 66 F-16V fighter jets from the US under the "Phoenix Rising" (Fengxiang) project, with deliveries originally scheduled to begin in 2023 and conclude by the end of 2026. However, it was not until October 2026 that the first two jets finally arrived. Reports also cite assessments from Taiwan indicating that the delivery of the full batch of 66 aircraft could be delayed until as late as the end of 2028. Even more strange is the fact that the two fighter jets remained in Hawaii for over a month before flying to Taiwan. Was it a technical issue, a supply chain problem, or something else? The Taiwan public remains in the dark. The arms procurement project, initially touted as a means to enhance defense capabilities, has instead been characterized by delivery delays, high costs, and a lack of transparency regarding progress. For Taiwan society, what exactly has been gained in exchange for such an exorbitant expenditure of taxpayers' money? What is the actual value of the so-called compensation measures? Who bears the costs resulting from the delay? The delayed arrival of merely two fighter jets can hardly be hailed as a "major victory." Why is the DPP so fervent? The reason the DPP authorities are displaying such high-pitched excitement is that they need to repackage a long-overdue arms delivery as a so-called "achievement in Taiwan island-US relations." In recent years, the DPP has persistently instilled the concept in Taiwan society that continued arms purchases from the US would guarantee greater security for the island. This sense of urgency to find a cover-up has been heightened by the DPP's alarm over the rising prevalence of "abandoning Taiwan" and "doubting the US" sentiments, particularly as China and the US have sought greater strategic stability in their relationship. Under this narrative, the arrival of two F-16Vs in Taiwan has been imbued with political significance that transcends the hardware itself. They are cited as proof of continued US support for Taiwan island and used to argue that the DPP’s strategy of "seeking independence by relying on the US" remains viable. The problem, however, is that while propaganda can alter news headlines, it cannot change the reality of "delayed delivery with reduced scale," let alone erase the inevitable fate of becoming a mere pawn when “seeking independence through reliance on external forces.” In arms procurement deals, Taiwan is forced to swallow the loss in silence The DPP authorities are spending a massive amount of money in the hope of acquiring a comprehensive set of capabilities, including the aircraft themselves, spare parts, weapon systems, software, maintenance and support, and personnel training. However, based on currently disclosed information, there appears to be no clear provision for liability regarding the delivery delays. The limited compensation Taiwan has managed to secure consists primarily of non-cash arrangements, such as extended warranties, additional spare parts, and technical services. This raises a practical issue: If the seller can initially deliver only a small fraction of the order without bearing clear liability for compensation – while the buyer continues to shoulder the costs associated with tied-up budgets, delayed training, and the disruption of operational readiness – then what kind of transaction is this? Furthermore, public opinion on the island has raised questions regarding whether the electronic warfare systems, navigation systems, and associated weaponry for the initial batch of fighter jets are fully in place; Taiwan's “defense” authorities need to provide a professional, transparent, and verifiable explanation. Against the backdrop of incomplete deliveries, the arrival of two fighter jets in Taiwan appears to be merely a symbolic gesture, devoid of any practical significance. No amount of arms spending can alter the balance of power between the two sides of the Taiwan Straits The DPP authorities are continuously ramping up arms purchases from the US, attempting to create a political illusion of "seeking independence through force" and "resisting reunification through force." However, the quantity of weapons does not equate to actual combat capability, nor do external arms sales equate to genuine security. Faced with the formidable, integrated, and modernized military might of the People's Liberation Army, the piecemeal weaponry procured by the Taiwan authorities from abroad cannot alter the overall balance of power between the two sides of the Taiwan Straits. Spending vast sums of public money on arms every year cannot change the political foundation of the Taiwan question, let alone halt the historical process of the motherland's reunification. So-called arms purchases essentially pin the safety and future of the residents of Taiwan on the commercial transactions and strategic calculations of external forces. US arms manufacturers prioritize their own interests; certain US politicians seek to consolidate their influence; and the DPP authorities use these deals to hype up a political narrative of "external support." It is Taiwan society that ultimately bears the cost. The residents of Taiwan must shoulder the burden of exorbitant military spending, delivery delays, equipment maintenance, and the price of escalating regional tensions, all while facing the risk of being pushed to the forefront of military confrontation. For Taiwan, increased arms purchases do not equate to peace. Placing orders with the US will not bring about ‘defense autonomy’ If the so-called "defense autonomy" repeatedly hyped by the DPP amounts to nothing more than constantly purchasing from the US and waiting indefinitely for delivery – while leaving Taiwan society to bear the consequences – then such "autonomy" is entirely a false proposition. True security can only be built upon clear strategic judgment, stable social development, a comprehensive industrial base, and the avoidance of escalating conflict. Blind reliance on external forces can neither substitute for Taiwan’s own governance capabilities nor resolve the fundamental issues between the two sides of the Taiwan Straits. The arrival of two F-16V jets in Taiwan may be newsworthy, but it should not serve as a fig leaf for the DPP authorities to evade issues. This belated and scaled-back delivery cannot be repackaged as "support for Taiwan," nor can it alter the future trajectory of cross-Straits relations. The more the DPP authorities cheer for the arrival of two belated fighter jets, the more they expose their anxiety over relying on foreign weaponry to sustain a false narrative. Faced with the formidable military might of the PLA and the disparity in overall strength between the two sides of the Taiwan Straits, no amount of foreign arms purchases can alter the big picture, let alone prop up the fantasy of "seeking independence through force." The true path to safeguarding the well-being of Taiwan compatriots lies in reducing confrontation, steering clear of the risk of war, and guiding cross-Straits relations back to the correct track of peaceful development. Weapons may be delivered, but fantasies will not thereby become reality; arms purchases may generate hype, but they cannot change the inevitable trend toward reunification.

item.title: The more turbulent the world becomes, the more precious a peaceful China is: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-30 00:27:00
A night view of the Wangfujing pedestrian street in Beijing on September 27, 2026. Photo: VCG Peace and security are defining features of China's governance and hallmarks of Chinese modernization. Peaceful China is a light that millions upon millions of Chinese people, secure in their daily lives, shine into a world that is far from peaceful. It safeguards the everyday lives of millions of families while contributing Chinese wisdom, Chinese solutions and Chinese strength to global security governance. A working conference on the Peaceful China Initiative was held in Beijing on Monday. A recent instruction made by Chinese President Xi Jinping was conveyed at the conference. In his instruction, Xi stated that since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, significant progress has been made in building a safe China, making the country one of the safest in the world. Notably, peace and security are defining features of China's governance and hallmarks of Chinese modernization. Throughout human history, no country or region has achieved modernization amid persistent turmoil. From the development of a nation to the well-being of every family, peace and security are indispensable. China now ranks among the countries with the lowest rates of criminal offenses and homicide and the fewest gun-related crimes. These three distinctions provide a solid foundation for the strong sense of security enjoyed by the Chinese people. Advancing the Peaceful China Initiative in a turbulent and rapidly changing world represents a weighty commitment. The 2026 Global Peace Index shows that global peacefulness has deteriorated for 12 consecutive years, while the number of active state-based conflicts worldwide has reached its highest level since the end of World War II. According to the latest report from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, as of the end of 2025, there were 117 million people forcibly displaced globally, equivalent to one in every 67 people on Earth. Meanwhile, Gallup's 2025 Global Safety Report showed that among 144 countries and regions surveyed, 94 percent of respondents in China said they feel safe walking alone at night. China has once again been recognized as one of the safest countries in the world and is the only major world power to make the list. In today's world, stability itself has become a scarce resource, and it is widely recognized as one of China's strengths. When foreign bloggers and visitors come to China, what often surprises them most is not the high-speed rail network or spectacular drone light shows, but the small details of everyday life that directly affect them: being able to go out for a late-night meal at 1 am, having a taxi driver return a phone left in the car, leaving a backpack at a café table while ordering and finding it still there upon returning, or seeing a young woman finish work, take the subway and then a bus, before walking another 10 minutes through a hutong or alley to get home. Scenes that might require suspenseful background music in an urban drama elsewhere are simply part of ordinary life in China. Data from China's National Immigration Administration showed that inbound trips made by foreign nationals exceeded 22.91 million in the first half of 2026, a surge of 20.4 percent year-on-year. There is a close connection between China's favorable public security environment and the continuing popularity of "China Travel." What particularly impresses many foreign visitors is that in China, security is not a privilege enjoyed by a small minority, but a basic public good accessible to the Chinese people. A peaceful China is no accident. It is the result of a combination of factors, including institutional strengths, governance effectiveness, cultural traditions and economic development. China's approach to security is people-centered, with development at its core. Poverty alleviation, medical insurance, social security, compulsory education and employment support all help give people confidence that their lives can continue to improve. From pushing to dismantle the "four major families" of criminal rings in northern Myanmar to better safeguarding food safety; from cracking down in accordance with the law on crimes targeting the elderly and children to continuously strengthening the public security prevention and control system; and from resolving disputes at their source to identifying and addressing public safety hazards, the advancement of the Peaceful China Initiative has continuously responded to people's evolving expectations for security. The results can be felt in people's everyday lives. Efforts to advance the Peaceful China Initiative to a higher level have extended into every urban community and every rural village, reaching the "last mile" of public security. The "Chinese sense of security" also stems from goodwill within society and a sense of civic responsibility found in the social atmosphere: Foreign tourists who lose their phones are able to get them back, and delivery workers report suspicious packages when they spot them. Recently, the positive perception that "Chinese people don't steal phones" has continued to gain traction on overseas social media, with foreign netizens recommending that wherever you travel in the world, look for a Chinese person first if you need someone to take your photo. Under the Peaceful China Initiative, China has not only become one of the world's safest major countries, but has also allowed the world to encounter more and more civic-minded Chinese people. Peaceful China is a light that millions upon millions of Chinese people, secure in their daily lives, shine into a world that is far from peaceful. It is the collective glow of more than 1.4 billion people that forms the strongest and the most dazzling foundation of a peaceful China. The more turbulent the world becomes, the more precious a peaceful China is. As a major country of more than 1.4 billion people, China unwaveringly implements a holistic approach to national security, maintains long-term social stability, and creates an environment in which people can live and work in peace and contentment - that itself is a significant contribution to global peace and security. A peaceful China is not only a shining national calling card, but also a vivid example of China promoting the building of a community with a shared future for humanity. It safeguards the everyday lives of millions of families while contributing Chinese wisdom, Chinese solutions and Chinese strength to global security governance.
